moment: The narrator establishes that Jacob Marley has been dead for seven years.
Bob Cratchit tries to warm himself at a candle because Scrooge will not let him add coal to his fire.
Fred visits Scrooge at work and invites him to Christmas dinner.
Scrooge refuses to give money to the charity collectors.
Scrooge frightens away a boy singing a Christmas carol by seizing his ruler.
Scrooge reluctantly gives Bob Cratchit Christmas Day off.
At home Scrooge sees Marley's face in his door knocker.
The bells in Scrooge's house ring, and Marley's ghost enters through the locked door.
Marley's ghost shows Scrooge his chain and warns him that three spirits will visit.
Scrooge looks out of his window and sees chained spirits who can no longer help the living.
The Ghost of Christmas Past appears beside Scrooge's bed.
Scrooge asks the spirit to cover the light shining from its head with its cap.
The spirit takes Scrooge to the country road where he grew up.
Scrooge recognises his old schoolfellows as they travel home for Christmas.
Scrooge sees himself as a lonely boy left at school over Christmas.
Scrooge joyfully recognises the storybook characters who kept him company in his childhood reading.
Scrooge wishes he had given something to the boy who sang a carol at his door.
Scrooge's sister Fan arrives at his school to bring him home.
Fan tells the young Scrooge that their father is kinder and has agreed to let him come home.
Scrooge becomes uneasy when the spirit reminds him that his nephew Fred is Fan's son.
The young Scrooge and Dick Wilkins clear Fezziwig's warehouse to make room for a Christmas party.
Fezziwig throws a Christmas party for his employees and friends.
Mr and Mrs Fezziwig lead an energetic dance at their Christmas party.
Scrooge defends Fezziwig by explaining that an employer's kindness can make workers happy.
After watching Fezziwig's party, Scrooge wishes he could speak to Bob Cratchit.
Belle tells the young Scrooge that a golden idol has taken her place in his affections.
Belle ends her engagement to Scrooge because money has become more important to him.
The spirit shows Scrooge Belle as a mother, surrounded by her lively children.
Belle's husband describes seeing Scrooge alone in his office while Marley lay dying.
After seeing Belle with her family, Scrooge presses the spirit's cap over its light.
Scrooge finds the Ghost of Christmas Present sitting among piles of festive food.
Scrooge tells the spirit that he is ready to learn from whatever it shows him.
In the streets, the spirit blesses Christmas dinners and restores good humour to people who quarrel.
At the Cratchits' house, Martha hides and then surprises Bob when he returns with Tiny Tim.
Bob explains that Tiny Tim hoped to remind churchgoers of Christ's healing miracles.
The spirit shows the Cratchits sharing Christmas dinner.
Mrs Cratchit brings in the Christmas pudding, and the whole family praises it.
After dinner, Tiny Tim offers a Christmas blessing for everyone.
The spirit warns that Tiny Tim will die if the future remains unchanged.
The spirit repeats Scrooge's words about the surplus population, leaving him ashamed.
Bob proposes a toast to Scrooge, and Mrs Cratchit objects.
Scrooge and the spirit visit a family of miners singing a Christmas song by their fire.
At a remote lighthouse, two keepers share a drink and wish each other a merry Christmas.
On a ship at sea, the crew remember Christmas and their loved ones at home.
At Fred's party, Scrooge hears his nephew express pity for him and promise to keep inviting him.
Scrooge is moved by a tune that was familiar to his sister Fan.
Scrooge watches Fred and his guests play a guessing game at their Christmas party.
Fred and his guests drink a toast to Scrooge and wish him a merry Christmas.
Scrooge notices that the spirit has grown old and learns that its life will end at midnight.
The spirit reveals two children named Ignorance and Want.
The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come approaches in a dark robe and points silently.
Businessmen discuss a man's death and joke about attending his funeral.
Two wealthy men briefly mention the death before turning their conversation to the weather.
Scrooge looks for his future self among the businessmen but finds another man in his usual place.
At Old Joe's shop, thieves sell belongings taken from the dead man.
Mrs Dilber sells sheets, towels, clothing and silverware stolen from the dead man's home.
The charwoman reveals that she took the dead man's bed-curtains while his body was still there.
The charwoman boasts that she even took the shirt intended for the dead man's burial.
Scrooge sees a dead man's covered body and cannot bring himself to lift the sheet.
Scrooge asks the spirit to show him someone who feels emotion at the man's death.
Caroline and her husband are relieved that their merciless creditor has died.
Scrooge asks to see tenderness connected with a death.
Scrooge visits the grieving Cratchits and learns that Tiny Tim has died.
Bob describes the green burial place he has visited and breaks down over Tiny Tim.
Bob tells his family that Fred has offered sympathy and help.
The Cratchits promise never to forget Tiny Tim or the patience and kindness he showed.
At Scrooge's former office, he sees unfamiliar furniture and another man in his place.
In the churchyard, Scrooge asks whether the future he has seen can still be changed.
Scrooge reads his own name on the gravestone and promises to change.
As Scrooge begs for a different future, the phantom shrinks into a bedpost.
Scrooge wakes in his own bed and realises he can still change his future.
Scrooge laughs and cries with joy as he gets dressed and wishes everyone a merry Christmas.
A boy tells Scrooge it is Christmas Day, and Scrooge sends a prize turkey to the Cratchits.
Scrooge pays for a cab to deliver the turkey and rewards the boy who fetched it.
Scrooge meets one of the charity collectors and promises a generous donation.
Scrooge goes to church and enjoys walking through the streets and speaking to people.
Scrooge joins Fred and his guests for Christmas dinner.
When Bob arrives late the next morning, Scrooge surprises him with a pay rise.
Scrooge promises to help Bob's family and tells him to make up the fires.
Tiny Tim survives, and Scrooge becomes like a second father to him.
